present-simple.title: Present Simple Tense
present-simple.formula: Subject + Base Verb (V1) (+ s/es for he/she/it)
present-simple.explanation: Used to describe habitual actions, universal truths, unchanging situations, and scheduled events.

examples.text: I work in London.
The sun rises in the east.
The train leaves at 6 PM.

commonMistakes: Forgetting -s/-es with third-person singular (e.g. 'He go' instead of 'He goes').

present-continuous.title: Present Continuous Tense
present-continuous.explanation: Used for actions happening right now at the moment of speaking or temporary situations.

examples.text: She is reading a book.
I am staying with my friend this week.

commonMistakes: Using continuous tense with stative verbs like 'know', 'like', 'want' (e.g. 'I am knowing').

present-perfect.title: Present Perfect Tense
present-perfect.explanation: Connects the past with the present: past actions with present consequences, life experiences, or unfinished time.

examples.text: I have lost my passport.
examples.note: Present result: I don't have it now

examples.text: She has visited Paris twice.

commonMistakes: Using specific past time expressions like 'yesterday' or 'in 2020' with present perfect.

present-perfect-continuous.title: Present Perfect Continuous
present-perfect-continuous.explanation: Emphasizes the duration of an activity that began in the past and is still continuing now.

examples.text: I have been waiting for two hours.

past-simple.title: Past Simple Tense
past-simple.explanation: Used for completed actions at a specific time in the past.

examples.text: We bought a new jacket yesterday.

commonMistakes: Using did + V2 in negatives or questions (e.g. 'did went' instead of 'did go').

past-continuous.title: Past Continuous Tense
past-continuous.explanation: Describes actions that were in progress at a specific time in the past.
usage: Action in progress in the past

examples.text: I was cooking when the phone rang.

past-perfect.title: Past Perfect Tense
past-perfect.explanation: Shows that an action happened before another action in the past ('the past of the past').

examples.text: The train had left before I reached the station.

commonMistakes: Overusing past perfect when a simple past sequence with 'then' is sufficient.

past-perfect-continuous.title: Past Perfect Continuous
past-perfect-continuous.explanation: Highlights the duration of an action up to a certain point in the past.
usage: Duration before a past point in time

examples.text: She had been studying for 3 hours before she took a break.

commonMistakes: Confusing with past continuous when duration is key.

future-simple.title: Future Simple Tense
future-simple.explanation: Used for spontaneous decisions, predictions without present evidence, and promises.

examples.text: I will call you tomorrow.

commonMistakes: Using 'will' for already planned arrangements instead of present continuous or going to.

future-continuous.title: Future Continuous Tense
future-continuous.explanation: Used for actions that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future.
usage: In progress at a future time

examples.text: This time tomorrow I will be flying to London.

future-perfect.title: Future Perfect Tense
future-perfect.explanation: Describes an action that will be completed before a specific point in the future.
usage: Action completed before a future deadline

examples.text: By next month, I will have finished my degree.

commonMistakes: Using 'has' with will (e.g. 'will has completed' is always wrong; must be 'will have').

future-perfect-continuous.title: Future Perfect Continuous
future-perfect-continuous.explanation: Emphasizes the duration of an activity up to a specific time in the future.
usage: Duration up to a future point

examples.text: By 2027, she will have been teaching here for 10 years.

commonMistakes: Extremely complex form; ensure 'will have been + ing' structure is preserved.

voice-passive.title: Passive Voice
voice-passive.formula: Subject (Recipient) + be + Past Participle (V3) (+ by Agent)
voice-passive.explanation: Used when the focus is on the action or the receiver of the action rather than who performed it.

examples.text: English is spoken worldwide.
The bill was paid by my father.

commonMistakes: Using base verb instead of V3 (e.g. 'was write' instead of 'was written').

conditional-zero.title: Zero Conditional
conditional-zero.explanation: Expresses general truths, scientific facts, and automatic results.

examples.text: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.

commonMistakes: Using 'will' in the result clause when expressing universal facts.

conditional-first.title: First Conditional
conditional-first.formula: If + Present Simple, will/can/may/should + Base Verb (V1)
conditional-first.explanation: Expresses a real, likely condition in the present or future with a probable outcome.

examples.text: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.

commonMistakes: Using 'will' in the if-clause (e.g. 'If it will rain' is incorrect).

conditional-second.title: Second Conditional
conditional-second.formula: If + Past Simple (were for be), would/could/might + Base Verb
conditional-second.explanation: Expresses an unreal, hypothetical, or improbable situation in the present or future.

examples.text: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.
If I were you, I would take that offer.

commonMistakes: Using 'would' in both clauses (e.g. 'If I would have money, I would buy').

conditional-third.title: Third Conditional
conditional-third.formula: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), would/could/might have + Past Participle (V3)
conditional-third.explanation: Refers to an impossible condition in the past and its imaginary past result (regret or relief).

examples.text: If you had told me earlier, I would have helped you.

polite-request.title: Polite Request Pattern
polite-request.explanation: Used to ask for help, information, or permission respectfully.

examples.text: Could you tell me how much this costs?

commonMistakes: Using 'Would you mind' followed by base verb instead of gerund (must be 'Would you mind helping').
